passages.text: Indeed, to take an immediate example (as I also said on another occasion), in the Caucasus Mountains the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out—the tomb of a savage tyrant and killer of his children. His son, named Zeus, became worse; appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic, he breaks up many marriages and punishes his father together with his uncles. When he then died, the Cretans point out his tomb. In Mesopotamia, a certain Helios lies at Hatra and a certain Selene at Carrhae; a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt; Ares in Thrace; Aphrodite in Cyprus; and Asclepius in Epidaurus. Tombs of many other such figures are also visible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although σῆμα can mean a sign or monument, the burial context and the subsequent τάφον and τάφοι support “tomb.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the alleged magical means and ἀναφανείς, which presents his world-rule as an appearance or emergence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν πατέρα σὺν τοῖς θείοις κολάζει
lexical_decisions.chosen: punishes his father together with his uncles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The family and mythological context supports the substantival sense “uncles,” with the father and uncles as joint objects. “Punishes his father together with the divine ones” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain Helios lies at Hatra
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἄτροις is treated as the dative plural place-name referring to Hatra in Mesopotamia.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The apposition explicitly identifies Hermes as a human being; the verb “lies” is carried forward from κεῖνται.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τελευτήσαντος τὸν τάφον Κρῆτες ἐπιδεικνῦσιν
source_issues.issue: The genitive absolute does not explicitly identify the person who died. The continuing focus and the Cretan tomb tradition favor Zeus; Cronus is grammatically possible but contextually less likely.

passages.text: Thus it has been plainly acknowledged by those who think correctly that they were human beings. Those who were their contemporaries, perceiving that they had proved mortal, paid less attention to them after they died; but the long passage of time clothed them with the reputation of gods. Do not be amazed if those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles were deceived, or those in the days of Dionysus or anyone else of that period, since the people in those places worship even Hector at Ilium and Achilles on the island of Leuce, the Opuntians worship Patroclus, and the Rhodians worship Alexander the Macedonian.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it has been plainly acknowledged that they were human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implied subjects are the allegedly divine figures discussed in the preceding section; the perfect construction identifies them as having been human.

lexical_decisions.chosen: perceiving that they had proved mortal
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can express noticing, apprehending, or suspecting, while the completed deaths demonstrate the figures’ mortality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: clothed them with the reputation of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the image of time placing divine repute around them without asserting that they truly became gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ κατὰ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Ἡρακλέα γενόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The surrounding argument concerns contemporaries and the effect of elapsed time. “Those associated with Asclepius and Heracles” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since the people in those places worship even Hector
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ὅπου introduces a striking supporting circumstance; the worshipers are supplied later by οἱ ἐκεῖ.

passages.text: But among the Egyptians, even now, a man is worshiped as a god before his death. This, at least, is a lesser act of impiety, because the Egyptians accord divine honors while a man is alive; but the most ridiculous thing of all is that they worship birds and reptiles and all animals. For most human beings neither understand nor do anything with judgment. Now observe what is most shameful of all: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans, whom most people call Zeus, they depict on a panel as a goose coupled with Leda and set up publicly. As retribution for this outrage, I would have liked it if they had portrayed their present king in a shameful coupling and, having done the same thing they have dared to do in Zeus’s case, had set it up publicly, so that, even if only through the anger of their temporary king—and he a human being—they might learn through punishment how due honor must be rendered. I tell you these things not as one who has already recognized the God who truly is, but, being fair-minded, I confess: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Egyptians accord divine honors
lexical_decisions.rationale: Νομίζω can denote customary observance or acknowledgment; here it concerns treating a living person as entitled to divine honors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν δι’ αὐτῶν ὄντα πατέρα θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase δι’ αὐτῶν is literally “through them.” In context it can mark Zeus’s status as established through their own representation or claim; “through their agency” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a goose coupled with Leda
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χῆνα explicitly means “goose,” not the familiar “swan.” The participle describes Zeus as joined or correspondingly formed with Leda and, in this sexual context, is rendered “coupled with.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a shameful coupling
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πλοκή can denote entwining or entanglement; the preceding sexual image involving Zeus and Leda supports “coupling.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: their temporary king
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πρόσκαιρος emphasizes that the earthly ruler lasts only for a limited time.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τί θεὸς οὐκ οἶδα, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε σαφῶς ὅτι θεός, νομίζω εἰδέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between not knowing what God is and knowing that God exists. “What sort of god” and “that he is God” are grammatically possible but fit the immediate contrast less directly.

source_issues.issue: The construction continues with aorist indicatives and is compressed. It defensibly expresses an unreal wish, “I would have liked it if they had ...”; “I wanted to see whether they had ...” is grammatically conceivable but fits the argument less well. No textual correction is required.

passages.text: To take an immediate example, the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God; neither can mixing, blending, coming-to-be, the visible vessel that encompasses the whole, the sediment collecting in Hades, the water floating on top, the boiling substance, or the air extending from it as far as the things here. For whether the four elements had stood apart from one another—in which case they could not have been mixed for the generation of a living creature without some great craftsman—or had always been joined to one another, even so they are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature, so that it may be able to preserve the proportion of each to each and may possess a well-bounded constitution, and so that all the things within may receive the appropriate harmony. Likewise, the craftsman mind precisely fashions the proper places of each with complete beauty. To sum up: of all the other things that a living creature must ever have, nothing was lacking in this great living creature of the whole circuit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ πρῶτα τέσσαρα στοιχεῖα θεὸς εἶναι οὐ δύναται τὰ ὑπὸ ἄλλου γενόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final participial phrase characterizes the four elements and supplies the reason they cannot themselves be God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the visible vessel that encompasses the whole
lexical_decisions.rationale: Κύτος denotes a hollow body, cavity, or vessel. “Vessel” preserves the cosmological container image without identifying it more specifically.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἐν τῷ ᾄδῃ συρρέουσα ὑποστάθμη
lexical_decisions.chosen: the sediment collecting in Hades
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment, dregs, or what settles at the bottom, while συρρέουσα presents it as flowing or gathering together.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐξ αὐτῆς μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διήκων ἀήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the air extending from it as far as the things here
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun most naturally refers to the immediately preceding “boiling substance,” though another feminine item in the list is grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον τῶν τοῦ ζῴου μελῶν καὶ μερῶν συναρμόζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: are fitted together to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes an intelligent fitting of the elements to the proper constitution or requirements of the creature’s members and parts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may possess a well-bounded constitution
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἕξις here denotes condition or constitution, while εὐπερίγραφος suggests being readily circumscribed or clearly bounded. “A well-defined constitution” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ ζῴῳ τῆς ὅλης περιφορᾶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: in this great living creature of the whole circuit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The cosmos is presented as a great living creature. Περιφορά can denote revolution, circular motion, or the circuit produced by it; “of the whole revolution” is also possible.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα τὴν ἑκάστου πρὸς ἕκαστον ἀναλογίαν ἀποσώζειν δύνηται καὶ τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ
source_issues.issue: The singular verbs leave their subject implicit. The resulting organized whole or living creature is the best contextual referent; the neuter plural elements can also govern singular verbs in Greek, so they remain a grammatical alternative.

passages.text: Thus there must be some unoriginated craftsman mind that either gathered the elements when they were apart or, when they were together with one another, skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature and completed a single work from them all; for it is impossible for an exceedingly wise work to be completed without some greater mind. Nor indeed can love be the craftsman of all, nor desire, nor force, nor anything else of that kind, since such things are passions and naturally come and go. Nor is whatever is borne by another a god, nor indeed whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unoriginated craftsman mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀγέννητος means not generated or not brought into being. “Unoriginated” suits the contrast with elements produced by another; “unbegotten” is possible but carries stronger traditional theological associations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb emphasizes artful or craftsmanlike arrangement, while the prepositional phrase states its purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an exceedingly wise work
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the work as embodying extraordinary wisdom or skill; “a work of surpassing skill” is an idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: love can be the craftsman of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἔρως can denote love as a cosmic principle and may evoke personified Eros. Lowercase “love” avoids requiring personification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάθη ὄντα συμβαίνειν καὶ ἀποβαίνειν πέφυκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: such things are passions and naturally come and go
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired verbs describe the proposed principles as contingent passions that arise and depart.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου φερόμενόν ἐστιν θεὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever is borne by another is a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation is negated by the preceding οὐδὲ. Φέρω in the passive can mean carried, borne, or moved; “moved by another” is also viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ὑπὸ χρόνου ἢ φύσεως ἀλλοιούμενον καὶ εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι ἀναλυόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the alteration, the image of dissolution, and its stated outcome of nonexistence.
